transcript:
Meeting Header: Date/Time: 2025-09-18 16:00 UTC | Duration: 70 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Atlas CTO), Priya (ML Platform Lead), Aisha (SRE), Ben (Data Scientist)

Summary: technical deep-dive focused on supporting >128k token contexts for Atlas Health workloads. Discussed runtime considerations: KV cache behavior for extremely long KV histories, chunking/streaming strategies, attention optimizations (sliding, local/global), batching tradeoffs, quantization impact on latency/throughput, and VPC/on-prem constraints for PHI.

Topics: long-context (128k+), chunking + stitch strategies, KV cache eviction & warm-starts, continuous batching, uncertainty around quantization (4-bit/8-bit) for clinical accuracy, private deployment (VPC/on-prem) network egress and kernel compatibility.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving time — appreciate it. Jordan and I will drive today, it's a slightly deep technical call. Quick intros?
[00:12] Carlos (Atlas): yeah, Carlos here, CTO. We run a clinical document synthesis platform, need to index and summarize patient histories up to — well potentially really long, like 100k to 200k tokens across threads. Our big asks: latency SLO under 1s per turn for small follow-ups, and ability to ingest full history for certain offline jobs.
[00:30] Priya (Atlas): priya here, leading the ML infra, we care about determinism, audit logs, and that quantization doesn't hallucinate clinical facts.
[00:40] Jordan (Redwood SE): great. quick framing: we've been running several 128k+ experiments with chunking and attention optimizations; there are a few patterns that work well in practice. we'll walk through runtime tradeoffs, KV cache semantics, and what Dedicated/Private look like.
[01:05] Ben (Atlas): quick clarifying q — when you say 128k experiments, is that single contiguous sequence or chunked windows stitched?
[01:15] Jordan: mostly chunked. single contiguous 128k in memory for transformer isn't practical unless you have specialty kernels and huge memory. what we do is a hybrid: chunk the long input into segments (e.g., 8k-32k windows), compute compressed representations and maintain a KV-layered cache that lets later prompts reference earlier summaries. there's nuance: attention patterns, global tokens, and re-embedding recent context.
[01:45] Maya: i'll drop the runbook link after the call — includes example chunking configs and a benchmark sheet.
[02:05] Priya: i'm concerned about the KV cache warm-start: if we evict older segments and then later need them, what's the rehydration latency? for clinical workflows we can't wait minutes.
[02:20] Jordan: good point. there are two modes — cold rehydrate from disk (s3 or local SSD) which can take seconds to tens of seconds depending on kv size and bandwidth; and, second, proactive prefetching heuristics. for Atlas we generally recommend a tiered cache: hot KV in GPU memory for last N segments, warm on local NVMe, cold on object storage. rehydration from NVMe is typically sub-second to low-second depending on size and parallelism.
[02:55] Aisha (Atlas SRE): that implies disk IO and potentially egress. For Private/on-prem we control NVMe sizing; for VPC (managed) we need to understand egress limits and whether Redwood Dedicated can avoid cross-AZ transfers.
[03:10] Jordan: yes — in Redwood Dedicated or Private we colocate storage with the serving workers; for hosted it's in our region but we can negotiate VPC peering for Private so there is no public egress. i'll annotate the private deployment doc with exact network patterns.
[03:40] Carlos: what about batching? our user-facing queries are low-latency but we also have offline batch summarization jobs for population health that can saturate throughput. how does continuous batching interact with long-context?
[03:55] Jordan: continuous batching is the runtime's approach to building large micro-batches over short windows to increase GPU utilization without hurting tail latency. with long-context, the big blocker is KV cache size per request which affects memory per batch element. we expose per-queue memory limits and batch shaping: you can prioritize low-latency queue (small batch, recent context only) and a background batch-optimizer for offline jobs. mixing those is about routing policies — small requests route to low-latency plane.
[04:30] Ben: any heuristics on chunk size? we have a lot of medical notes with dense token sequences, would smaller chunks blow up total compute?
[04:45] Jordan: there's a sweet spot. for many LLMs 8k-16k per chunk balances attention cost and number of forward passes. For very dense content, larger chunks (32k) reduce stitching artifacts but increase per-chunk O(n^2) attention cost unless you use efficient attention kernels. we recommend profiling: start 8k with overlapping margins (e.g., 256-512 tokens) and a summary/embedding index per chunk to prune search.
[05:20] Maya: note: we include example configs in the runbook and a benchmarking sheet; Jordan will share kernel/quantization notes.
[05:40] Priya: quantization — we can't degrade clinical accuracy. is 4-bit safe?
[05:50] Jordan: depends. quantization (GPTQ, LLM.int8(), etc) often preserves emergent behavior but edge-case factual accuracy can suffer. our approach: mixed precision and per-layer quant profiles. for atlas we can do A/B evals on your eval set; often 8-bit or mixed 4/8-bit with calibration preserves quality while cutting memory ~2x/3x. we also run calibration passes and fidelity evals that we can share.
[06:25] Carlos: any known breakages — hallucinations specifically tied to quant? we can't accept new clinical hallucinations.
[06:35] Jordan: yes sometimes logits drift on rare tokens. recommended mitigation: keep critical final layers in fp16, quantize middle layers; ensemble scores and reranking with a high-fidelity verifier model. we can instrument the pipeline to flag low-confidence tokens and fall back to a higher-precision run.
[07:00] Aisha: on the Private deployment side, what are the kernel constraints? we run on our own DGX pods, and want to use Redwood runtime — will your kernel selection play well with A100-80GB+SXM and H100?
[07:15] Jordan: absolutely we currently support A100/H100 variants; kernel selection is done at compile time based on sm capability. some high-memory, long-context kernels require patched CUDA and specific NCCL versions; we'll share a compatibility matrix. For H100 there are additional TF32/CUDA 12 notes.
[07:40] Ben: talk about attention optimizations — sliding attention, local/global mix?
[07:50] Jordan: two main families: sparse-local (sliding window) and global tokens. sliding/local reduces O(n^2) to O(n*w) where w is window size. for long-document retrieval we combine local windows for per-chunk coherence and a small set of global tokens for cross-chunk references. there's also block-sparse and token-merging (e.g., clustered attention) approaches. these require model-level support or compilation-time fusions we do in the runtime.
[08:35] Priya: what's the impact on latency vs throughput for those?
[08:40] Jordan: sliding attention reduces compute significantly for very long sequences so throughput improves, but depending on kernel it may increase latency slightly due to extra kernel launches. overall it's a net win for 128k contexts because naive full attention would be infeasible.
[09:05] Carlos: any real-world numbers? like tokens/sec or latency for a 128k retrieval+stitch request?
[09:12] Jordan: sample from our internal benchmarks: with chunking (16k windows, overlap 512), NVMe-backed warm cache, and mixed 8-bit quant, we saw end-to-end response for a small follow-up (context lookup + 512 token generation) about 400-800ms p50 on H100 dedicated instances; offline batch summarization at high parallelism achieved ~200k tokens/sec aggregated. caveat: these numbers vary a lot with model family and prompt complexity.
[09:50] Maya: also remember routing rules — low-latency plane will keep fewer KV segments in memory to hit sub-second.
[10:05] Aisha: security — audit logs and KMS. for PHI we need CMEK and HSM-based keys, and an audit trail for every inference. how granular are your logs and do they leave the VPC for Private?
[10:20] Jordan: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and can encrypt KV at rest with CMEK. audit logs are configurable; for Private they stay within your VPC. hosted Dedicated also supports private networking and limited export; will confirm details in security doc.
[10:45] Priya: what about deterministic replay for audits? can we snapshot KV states per request?
[10:55] Jordan: yes we can persist KV states and metadata for deterministic replay; retention is configurable and we have checksum-based integrity checks. keep in mind storage costs for full snapshots at 128k scale.
[11:15] Ben: a practical question: chunk stitching — do you recompute cross-chunk attention at inference time or do you rely on summaries/embeddings?
[11:25] Jordan: usually summaries/embeddings + a small global attention set. recomputing full cross-chunk attention is expensive; instead we do two-pass approaches: first retrieval over chunk embeddings to find relevant chunks, then a final pass where those chunks and the recent context are concatenated for generation. For very strict coherence you can do progressive refinement passes but those increase cost.
[12:00] Carlos: for our use-case we'd like hard guarantees: if follow-up references an old fact, latency must be low. sounds like we need hot KV for those patient timelines. how much memory per patient roughly?
[12:12] Jordan: depends on chunk size and embedding compressions. rough ballpark: with 16k chunks and 1k tokens per chunk average, per-chunk KV can be ~40-60MB in fp16; with quantization and compression you can get that down to 15-25MB. so for a patient with 10 chunks that's a couple hundred MB. we'll provide a sizing calculator.
[12:45] Maya: we'll include the sizing calc in the runbook and Jordan will run Atlas's sample through our benchmark.
[13:05] Priya: would love to see the kernel selection notes and if we need to rebuild torchvision or other libs for H100.
[13:15] Jordan: yes, compatibility matrix and recommended docker images included. note: some customers want deterministic kernels which requires pinned driver versions.
[13:30] Carlos: any gotchas with multi-tenant Dedicated? we prefer isolated workloads but want to share capacity sometimes.
[13:40] Maya: Dedicated offers node pools; you can pin model versions and node affinity. multi-tenancy isolation uses cgroup/rdma configs and eBPF for accounting. for regulated data we generally recommend Private with VPC peering.
[14:05] Ben: can we do an A/B on quant versus fp16 on our eval set?
[14:12] Jordan: yes — next steps: you send sample eval set and we'll run A/B with 4/8/fp16 and produce fidelity and latency tables.
[14:25] Aisha: on networking, one last ask: can we keep all traffic internal and avoid cloud egress logging?
[14:32] Jordan: yes for Private deployments; for Dedicated we can set up VPC peering and private routes to avoid public egress. will document.
[14:45] Maya: wrapping up — recap of action items (see metadata) and we'll schedule the pilot kickoff once we get the samples.
[14:55] Carlos: thanks, this was useful.
[15:00] Priya: thanks everyone.

References & links mentioned: runbook + benchmarks (internal): https://redwood.internal/runbooks/long-context-128k (shared post-call). Private deployment notes: https://redwood.internal/private-deployments (will annotate). Kernel compatibility matrix (to be shared).

End of transcript.
